messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leilani is a 20-year-old married interior designer who came to treatment several months after a pattern of physical assaults by her husband had culminated in a night she now experiences as both vivid and strangely unreachable. During an argument in their apartment, he had cornered her in a dark hallway, shouting inches from her face before hitting her. What remains most charged for her is not a complete story she can tell from beginning to end, but fragments tied to sensation: his voice suddenly getting louder, the feeling of being trapped with a man between her and the exit, the sight of him afterward as if danger were still attached to his body. Those details make her present triggers feel immediately understandable. A slammed door in a client’s home, a male contractor lingering with her in a room, or unexpectedly seeing her husband can pull her back into the same state before she has time to think.

Since then, loud noises and being alone with men do not just upset Leilani; they push her into ways of managing that have steadily narrowed her life. If a site visit requires walking through a dim unfinished space, she finds a reason to stay near the entrance or asks someone else to check measurements. At work she avoids being alone in a room or building, timing her movements so she is always near a receptionist, assistant, or another designer. When something sets her off, she goes over and over what she must have done wrong, blaming herself for staying, for not seeing it coming, for not leaving sooner. The same triggers also bring an immediate bodily alarm. A dropped sample book or raised male voice leaves her superalert, shoulders tight, heart racing, scanning the room and then glancing behind her as if someone might be coming up on her. Just as quickly, these moments stir the memory system that troubles her most: she may suddenly feel the whole emotional force of that night without any clear picture, or she tries to describe what happened and loses the thread, overcome by guilt as she speaks.

Those trigger moments also seem to confirm what she has come to believe about herself and the world. When she freezes around male clients or feels herself recoil at seeing her husband, she thinks, with a kind of finality, that her life has been destroyed by what happened. She feels cut off from other people her age and from the person she was before, as though she no longer belongs anywhere. Underneath that is a hard mistrust: people cannot be trusted, especially when they appear calm and familiar.

These beliefs keep her body in a constant state of preparedness. Because she is certain that people are unsafe and that she is no longer protected by ordinary closeness, she enters most spaces already on guard. She sits facing doors, checks behind her in parking garages and hallways, and notices every shift in tone from men on job sites. The same beliefs shape the way she remembers. When she tries to put the assaults into words, the account collapses into guilt-laden fragments; it is as if her mind returns not to a coherent narrative but to a conclusion that she was foolish, damaged, and abandoned from any place of safety.

Her memories in turn drive much of what she does to cope. When the emotional intensity arrives without an image, she avoids dark rooms, avoids being alone in buildings, and tries not to be in circumstances that resemble that hallway. After any attempt to recall the abuse, she ruminates for hours about her own responsibility. The memories also intensify her sense of danger: after a fragment or bodily surge, she becomes even more watchful, more tense, more likely to turn around repeatedly. And because each incomplete recollection is saturated with guilt, it leaves her more convinced that the trauma has ruined her life, that she belongs nowhere, and that trust is naïve. In a cruel way, the memory itself has made the world easier to trigger; loud noises, male presence, and seeing the offender now feel linked to something unfinished and undefended inside her.

Over time, the strategies she relies on have made her world smaller and more threatening. Avoiding dim spaces and refusing to be alone in rooms at work have begun to affect her credibility as a designer, especially when projects require independent walkthroughs or meetings with male vendors. She has become preoccupied with arranging her day around perceived safety, and the constant self-blame leaves her feeling even more isolated and alien from others. The more she avoids, the less chance she has to learn that every dark room, every man, every sudden sound is not that night again; instead, each avoidance preserves the trigger. Her vigilance rises with this shrinking of her life, and the effort to stay safe has itself become exhausting.

Leilani finally sought help after having to leave a client meeting when a contractor dropped a metal ladder and the crash sent her into full-body panic. She could not explain to her supervisor what had happened; she started, lost the thread, and was overwhelmed by shame. What frightens her most is the sense that this is permanent—that she will always live braced for danger, unable to trust anyone, unable to feel at home anywhere. What she hopes, more quietly, is to be able to work, to enter a room by herself, and to remember what happened without feeling that the memory itself proves her life is over.
